content.title: Bubble sort with stable duplicates
content.subject: dsa
content.source: Candidate-reported interview question, confirmed by the contributor; not an official company publication. References: LTM-035.
content.attribution: AI-assisted PrepPilot editorial adaptation; original source wording preserved separately. Not human-reviewed.
content.prompt:
Editorial adaptation, not the exact interview specification.

Return an ascending copy of an integer array using adjacent swaps and an early-stop flag. Length 0–1000; values −10000 through 10000. Trace [3,1,2,1], and explain empty, singleton and already sorted inputs. Do not mutate the input.
content.explanation: Passes: [1,2,1,3], then [1,1,2,3], then no swaps. Swap only when the left value is greater; equal values do not cross, so the algorithm is stable. Empty/singleton need no comparisons. Best case O(n), worst O(n²); the copy uses O(n) space.

content.title: Longest substring without repeated ASCII characters
content.subject: dsa
content.source: Candidate-reported interview question, confirmed by the contributor; not an official company publication. References: COG-093.
content.attribution: AI-assisted PrepPilot editorial adaptation; original source wording preserved separately. Not human-reviewed.
content.prompt:
Editorial adaptation, not the exact interview specification.

Return (length,start) of the longest contiguous substring with no repeated characters; choose earliest start on ties. ASCII length 0–2000; spaces and case matter. Empty input returns (0,0). Trace abba, abcabcbb and aaaa; give a linear-time algorithm.
content.explanation: Maintain last-seen indices and a left boundary. Set left=max(left,lastSeen[c]+1), then record c's index. Update the best only for a strictly longer window. abba → (2,0), abcabcbb → (3,0), aaaa → (1,0). Never move left backwards. O(n) time, O(128) space.

content.title: Find a weak peak by binary search
content.subject: dsa
content.source: Candidate-reported interview question, confirmed by the contributor; not an official company publication. References: COG-089.
content.attribution: AI-assisted PrepPilot editorial adaptation; original source wording preserved separately. Not human-reviewed.
content.prompt:
Editorial adaptation, not the exact interview specification.

For a nonempty array of 1–1000 integers, return any index whose value is at least each existing neighbor. Endpoints have one neighbor; duplicates allowed. Give an O(log n) algorithm, trace [1,3,2], [2,2], [1], and explain monotone inputs.
content.explanation: With inclusive low/high, compare mid with mid+1. If the latter is greater, set low=mid+1; otherwise high=mid. An ascending edge leads toward a weak peak; the other half also retains a weak peak. Return low. Example indices 1,0,0. Increasing arrays return last; decreasing arrays return first. O(log n) time, O(1) space. Weak-peak semantics are an editorial clarification.

content.title: Salary ranking, ties and NULL
content.subject: cs
content.source: Candidate-reported interview question, confirmed by the contributor; not an official company publication. References: LTM-078, LTM-079, COG-077.
content.attribution: AI-assisted PrepPilot editorial adaptation; original source wording preserved separately. Not human-reviewed.
content.prompt:
Editorial adaptation, not the exact interview specification.

PostgreSQL 18: employees(id integer PRIMARY KEY,name text,salary integer NULL). Rows (1,A,100),(2,B,200),(3,C,200),(4,D,NULL),(5,E,150). Write queries for all highest-paid employees and all employees with the second DISTINCT salary. Compare RANK, DENSE_RANK and ROW_NUMBER. Explain all-NULL and single-distinct-salary cases.
content.explanation: Highest: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary=(SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees); IDs 2,3. Second: WITH ranked AS (SELECT *,DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL) SELECT id,name,salary FROM ranked WHERE r=2; ID 5. Non-NULL ranks are RANK 1,1,3,4; DENSE_RANK 1,1,2,3; ROW_NUMBER with id as an additional tie-breaker 1,2,3,4. All-NULL gives neither result; one distinct salary gives no second. Row order is unspecified unless ORDER BY is used.

content.title: Choose an index from a workload
content.subject: cs
content.source: Candidate-reported interview question, confirmed by the contributor; not an official company publication. References: LTM-062, LTM-073.
content.attribution: AI-assisted PrepPilot editorial adaptation; original source wording preserved separately. Not human-reviewed.
content.prompt:
Editorial adaptation, not the exact interview specification.

PostgreSQL 18 orders(id integer PRIMARY KEY,customer_id integer NOT NULL,status text,created_at timestamp NOT NULL) receives frequent writes. Main query filters customer_id by equality, orders created_at descending and takes 20 rows. Propose one candidate index, discuss supported predicates, write cost and how to validate it.
content.explanation: Candidate: CREATE INDEX ON orders(customer_id,created_at DESC). Its leading key supports customer equality and ordered timestamps within that customer. It does not guarantee efficient date-only or status-only access. The primary key already indexes id. Every maintained index costs writes and storage. Compare EXPLAIN plans and measured workload behavior on representative data before deployment; no speedup is promised. Avoid indexing every column by default.

concerns: Proposed cohesive practice set; novice timing has not been measured. Hold if it takes less than 15 minutes rather than padding it.

content.title: Work rates with a staged team
content.subject: aptitude
content.attribution: AI-assisted original PrepPilot exercise and worked answer; pending human editorial review.
content.prompt: A completes a job in 12 hours, B in 18 hours, at constant independent rates. They work together for 3 hours, then A leaves. Find fraction completed, remaining time for B and total elapsed time. Compare with both working throughout, then explain why averaging 12 and 18 is invalid.
content.explanation: Combined rate 1/12+1/18=5/36 per hour. In 3 hours:5/12 done;7/12 remains. B takes (7/12)×18=10.5 more hours; total13.5 hours. Together throughout:36/5=7.2 hours. Completion times are reciprocals of rates, so their arithmetic mean is not a combined completion time.
